note: Every source this archive has put a name to, whether or not it gave anything back. A search that returns nothing is a result: without it the next person repeats the work, and — worse — reads a silence as an absence. “Blocked” means a login wall, a bot check or an access denial this archive has chosen not to get round. “Not yet” means known, wanted, and not obtained. The register is kept by hand in sources/searched.json and validated by tools/searched.py.
cols: What it gave, or did not

rows.src: Arcanum Digitheca — Šumbul, Šambul and Marić at Otočac
rows.what: Ahnentafel 11's family — the one person on the direct line with nothing but a name
rows.got:
**Nothing, and the nothing is informative.** *«Šumbul» Otočac* returns **0**. *«Šambul»* returns 348 hits and every one is a **Moroccan legionnaire tried at Cluj in 1936**. *«Marić» Otočac* returns 149, all twentieth-century passport notices, none of them ours.

**Marić is too common a surname for a press search without a given name and a date** — which is precisely why the odd first element of her name matters. See the next row.

rows.src: Ahnentafel 11 — «Ana Shambul Marić», and what to open next
rows.what: How to draw Tereza Žubrinić's mother's family, planned while FamilySearch is blocked
rows.got:
**She is the emptiest person on the direct line** — a name, two tree links, and nothing else. Her father is a **surname with no given name**; her mother **is not in the tree at all**.

**The name is probably not her name.** MyHeritage carries her as *«Ana Shambul Marić»* and, elsewhere, *«rođen Shumbul Marić»*. This archive has seen that shape before: the **nadimak**, the household name written beside the surname and underlined by the priest — *Antich Papa*, *Jellichich dictis Jurešina*. **«Shumbul Marić» looks like a by-name flattened into a double surname by a tree program.** If so the surname to search is **Marić**, and **Šumbul** is the house name — the only thing separating this family from every other Marić in Lika. *(Hypothesis. It is deliberately not being added to the by-names data, which holds only phrases read off a page.)*

**What is reachable, cheapest first.** The couple's children are Lucca (1853), Marija (about 15 Sept 1858), Jacobus and Tereza (1867); **Otočac births are filmed 1834–1858**. So **Lucca's and Marija's baptisms are both inside the book** — and the Otočac entries already read name the mother with her maiden surname and fix the household by village and **house number**. Then **Ana's own baptism**, about 1834–1838, which names **both her parents** — two walls in one entry. Then the **Stanje duša**, where a Marić household would appear with dates of birth for everyone in it.

**What is not reachable, and is said so:** their **marriage** (by 1852; the Otočac marriage film begins 1859) and **Tereza's own baptism** of 1867 (the birth film stops at 1858).

**And one thing to check before building on any of it:** Nikola was **nineteen** when Lucca was born. That is possible, and it is also the shape of a wrong attachment — the same confusion as the two men called Michaël in question 4d.

rows.src: FamilySearch — the Karlobag marriage register 1804–1861, located
rows.what: Ahnentafel 54's marriage — the document that would name his father and fix his age
rows.got:
**The block lifted for about fifteen minutes, and that was enough to put the book on the map.**

**The Karlobag marriages 1804–1861 are images ~228–258**, blanks to about 272, **END OF ITEM at 274**. Year map read off the page headers: **231 = 1807**, **232 = 1808/09**, **233 = 1811**, **234 = 1814**, **246 = 1843**.

**So ahnentafel 54's marriage is in images 230–233.** Maria Gerkacs was born August 1789 and their daughter on 23 April 1810, which puts the wedding in **1806–1809** — a four-image window in a book now located to the image. It is the document that would **name his father** and **fix his age**, which is the one thing standing between this archive and his death.

**And the volume has an index at the front**, images **~217–226** — left pages blank, the writing in a column beside the gutter. **Not read**: the block fell on the first crop of it. If it is like the death index it is the whole job in one page.

Two entries seen in passing and neither claimed: an 1807 marriage naming *«Matthææ filiæ defuncti **Josephi Smojver**… in Ledenik»* — **Smojver is a direct-line surname here** — and an 1808/09 one naming *«Matthææ filiæ defuncti **Martini U[roda?]**»*, where the surname is **not confirmed**.

**The second block behaved exactly as the note predicts:** image 231 answered, and ninety seconds later the same ark returned 403. One request, one answer, stop.

rows.src: FamilySearch — the Karlobag death register 1804–1861, and its index
rows.what: Ahnentafel 54's death — and an alphabetical index nobody knew was on the film
rows.got:
**The film carries an alphabetical index to the deaths** — images ~168–192, a printed letter at the head of each column, *Cognomen et Nomen | dies | mensis | annus | folium*. It turns a fifty-seven-year register into a lookup, and this archive did not know it was there. Its folio numbers were spot-checked twice and were right both times.

Under **U** it lists **fourteen Uroda deaths between 1808 and 1846**, with day, month, year and page.

**Ahnentafel 55 is confirmed to the year, and her husband gets a trade.** Folio 52, 6 August 1834: *«**Maria uxor piscatoris Georgii Uroda annorum 45**, … die 7ª hujus sepultum est Carlobagi in cœmeterio communi»*. The date is the tree's exactly, the age is the tree's exactly — born about 1789, and her baptism was read in August 1789 — and **she is *uxor*, not *vidua***.

**That one word did an afternoon's work.** Her husband was alive on 6 August 1834, which **rules out** the Georgius Uroda who died in 1808 and the Georgius Uroda who died in **1817** — the obvious answer, the one a hurried reader takes.

**Ahnentafel 54 is not settled, and is not being claimed.** Folio 66, 11 January 1846: *«Georgius Uroda **annorum 72, piscator**»* — same name, same trade, the only Georgius to die after his wife. But 72 in 1846 means born about **1774**, and the tree says **22 April 1777**, which would make him 68. **Three years out.** The other candidate is worse: *Joannes Uroda, **civis**, annorum 59*, 8 December 1843 — seven years out, and a citizen rather than a fisherman.

What would settle it is the **Karlobag marriage register 1804–1861**, on the same film, still unopened: it would name his father and fix his age at marriage.

And if the 1846 man is him, the census household becomes legible — **Uroda Maria vid., born 18 March 1789**, keeping Ive (1811), Vicko (1816) and Kate Maria (1820), who bracket ahnentafel 27 of 1810. A second wife, and his grown children. **A reconstruction, not a reading.**

rows.src: FamilySearch — the Karlobag Stanje duša, the U section
rows.what: Ahnentafel 54's household — the Urode of Karlobag
rows.got:
**Three Uroda households, at images 64 and 65, and ahnentafel 54 is in none of them.**

The book's order finally made sense: it is alphabetical **once**, images 8 to about 75, and the two pages of an opening run on from each other — *Pavicich, Perpich, Pilepich, Potocnjak, Rukavina, Šegota, Smojver, Tomljanović, **Uroda**, Uzelac, Vujačić*. What follows image 76 is not a second census but **later additions**, households entered as they formed, some running into the 1870s. **That corrects what this archive published an hour earlier.**

· **Uroda Jone** (image 64 left) — a household entered with a **brother and a sister** beside the head, and **four children dead in ten years**, the deaths written into the margin in Croatian months: *† 22 svibnja 1853, † 6 sept. 1852, † 19 sept. 1855, † 5 Aug. 1862*.
· **Uroda Maria vid.**, **18 March 1789** (image 64 right) — with Ive (1811), Vicko (1816), Kate Maria (1820).
· **Uroda Jure** (image 65 left) — with Franica (1832) and Fedorija (1839).

**The near-miss is the part worth keeping.** An Uroda widow born in 1789 is exactly what **ahnentafel 55** would look like — Maria Gerkacs, who married an Uroda and was born in 1789. Five months apart, same surname, same small town. **It is not her:** the tree gives her a death on **6 August 1834**, ten years before this book was opened. Right surname, right year, right town, wrong woman — and what caught it was a death date the tree had and the census did not.

**Nobody in the three households was born in 1777.** Ahnentafel 54 would have been sixty-seven. His absence puts his death **before 1844** — which puts it inside the **Karlobag death register 1804–1861**, on film and unopened. That is now the cheapest unopened document on this line.

And **Ive, Vicko and Kate Maria** are the right generation and town to be **ahnentafel 27's brothers and sister**. Candidates, not kin: what would join them is her marriage, in the Karlobag marriage register 1804–1861 — also on film, also unopened.

rows.src: FamilySearch — the Karlobag Stanje duša, read
rows.what: The household census, opened for the first time, and searched for the Pilipići
rows.got:
**Ahnentafel 13 has brothers and sisters.**

Image 48, right-hand page, first family — written *Pilepich*, the parish's own spelling:

**Pilepich Vicko, 17 Nov. 805** · **Matia ux., 23 April 810** · Joso f., 14 Oct. 835 · **Matia f., 18 Sept. 838** · Vice f., 16 Febr. 847 · Jure f. · Maria Jurka f., 24 *lipnja* 852.

**Three of those are the direct line and all three agree to the day** — ahnentafel 26, 27 and 13. **Four are new.** This archive had *no siblings at all* for ahnentafel 13; it now has a household of seven. The youngest child's month is written in **Croatian** (*lipnja*) inside a book with Latin headings.

The census does not give an age, it gives a **date of birth to the day**, and it carries **one communion column per year** from 1844 — so a household can be watched year by year.

A second Pilipić household sits below it: **Pilepich Maria ved., 7 April 789**, with six more, among them an **Oliva** — the given name of ahnentafel 53, recurring. Two further Pilipić households are on the facing page and on image 49. **Four Pilipić households in one small town**, none yet joined to another by a document. The openings either side are **Perpić**, a surname this archive knows from Krivi Put, forty kilometres away.

**Two things this archive said about the book yesterday were wrong, and both are corrected.** It is ordered by **family** number, not house number — Karlobag's registers of this period use no house numbers at all, and the 1838 baptism, re-read the same day, gives none either. And on the ordering — corrected again in the second sitting below — the book runs alphabetically **once**, images 8 to about 75; what follows is not a second census but **later additions**, households entered as they formed, some carrying dates into the **1870s**.

Finding the household took a survey of the whole film: there is **no index**, and the house-number route in was a dead end. Reading the rest is about a hundred openings and would give a **dated census of the whole town, twice, thirty years apart.**

rows.src: FamilySearch — the three Karlobag films, opened and range-checked
rows.what: What years Karlobag's films actually cover — four walls said “not checked”
rows.got:
**The label holds, and this time that is the good news.** Karlobag is the best-read parish in this archive and its ranges had never once been checked — three `unknown`s in the parish table, and four walls on the chart reading *«ranges not checked»*, which looks like a gap and is really an unopened door.

All three films were opened: **327 images** of births in two bound volumes (HDA 426 and 427), **435 images** carrying the 1804–1861 books *and* the older **marriages 1736–1804** and **deaths 1774–1804**, and **122 images of a Church Census this archive did not know existed**.

Read off the film, not the label: image 4 is **1723** and image 6 is the **1690s** — the front leaves are not in chronological order. Image 140 is **1761**, image 220 **1782**, image 260 **1792**. On the second film, image 300 is the **marriages of 1767** and image 360 the **deaths of 1775**. The language changes under you: **Croatian prose to the 1750s, Latin after, tabular from about 1780.**

**Four walls became reachable** — Jacob Pilipić about 1741, Georgi Uroda about 1750, Vicentius Luckinić about 1700, and **Josiph Smojver Vukić's own baptism of 1731**. **A fifth is answerable in a different way:** *Maria Uroda* is on the chart under her husband's surname, and you cannot search for a name you do not have — but **her marriage of about 1775 is inside the film**, and a marriage entry names the bride's father. *Maria Luckinić* misses by eleven years: her marriage falls about 1725 and the book begins in 1736.

And the **Stanje duša** is the prize nobody was looking for: a **date of birth to the day** for every soul, and a communion column for **every year from 1844**. It was read the same day — see the next row — and two things said here first were **wrong**: it is ordered by *family* number, not house number, and it is not one census but two.

rows.src: Arcanum Digitheca — the Hungarian press and official publications
rows.what: Fifteen queries across this family's surnames and the Hungarian names of its towns
rows.got:
**Lika and the Kvarner were administered from Budapest, this archive's own place strings still say so — *Ledenice, Modruš-Fiume, Magyarország* — and nobody in this estate had ever run a search in that administration's press.** One afternoon in it produced:

· **A number for the tobacco factory.** *A Pallas nagy lexikona* (1897): Zengg's *dohánygyára* **120 munkás**. *Révai Nagy Lexikona* (1926): **500 munkás**. This archive's most-quoted finding — the brides' occupation column going from three of five in 1909 to seven of eight in 1919 — now has the arithmetic behind it. **A four-fold factory in a town of a few thousand.**

· **A Žubrinić who kept a bank's cash.** *Magyar Compass* 1908: the **Srpska štedionica of Otočac**, founded 1904, *Kassier* **Venzeslav Žubrinić**. A merchant, **Daniel Žubrinić, Handelsmann in Otočac**, in the *Wiener Zeitung* of 1862. And a **Daniel Žubrinić, priest of the Senj-Modruš diocese**, posted to Otočac in 1885 — the very diocese whose registers this archive reads.

· **A man born at Otočac in 1886**, in three Austrian papers at once: *Mijo Zubrinic … 1886 geboren, aus Otocac, Kom. Lika-Krbava.* The archive holds **nobody** born at Otočac between 1875 and 1900.

· **A patronymic in a gazette** — *Službeni list*, 1966: **“Zubrinić Franje iz Prozora sina Jure”**, Općinski sud Otočac.

· **Three Kalanj men of Brinje in the First World War casualty lists**, with birth years and fates — Ivan b. 1891 a prisoner at Prokuplje, Franjo b. 1893 killed 6 March 1915. **This archive had never opened a First World War record.**

· **A third emigration.** *Feldkircher Anzeiger*, 1902: **Blaževići of Staroselo, Krmpote, working as masons in Vorarlberg**, with birth years and home commune. The archive knew America and Australia. It did not know about the Alps.

Everything is a **snippet**: Arcanum gives the text and paywalls the page image, so **none of it has been read at the page**, and none of it is in the tree.

rows.src: Arcanum Digitheca — Šumećica, and Senj in 1943
rows.what: The two queries that were supposed to matter most
rows.got:
**Both returned nothing, and both nothings are worth having.**

**Šumećica** — the hamlet the American manifests made important, and the birthplace of ahnentafel 10 — **appears nowhere in the Hungarian press.** A place can be central to a family and invisible to an empire.

**Senj 1943** returns nothing to this press, and that is not a silence about the raid: **the raid falls under the Italian occupation, after Hungarian administration ended.** This is the wrong press for it. The right one — the Italian occupation press, or Arolsen — has still to be opened.

Also recorded so nobody repeats it: the Hungarian spelling **«Blazsevics» returns 2,168 hits and almost every one is a modern footballer.**

rows.src: Arcanum Digitheca — the page images behind the snippets
rows.what: Reading any of the fifteen documents at the page rather than in extract
rows.got:
**«You have no active subscription.»** Arcanum returns the full-text snippet free and paywalls the scan. Every quotation this archive has taken from it is therefore an **extract with the OCR's own errors left in**, and is labelled that way rather than tidied — a cleaned-up quotation would claim a reading that did not happen.

The paywall is recorded, not worked around. What it costs is precise: the *Magyar Compass* entry for the Otočac savings bank would give the **whole board**, and the casualty lists would give the **house numbers** beside the Kalanj birth years.

rows.src: Find a Grave — every ZUBRINICH memorial on earth
rows.what: All 72, transcribed with cemetery, plot and dates, and matched against this archive
rows.got:
**The first cemetery source this archive has ever used, and it gave a woman her dates.**

John Zubrinich lies at Port Pirie in **CC, Lot 26**, and beside him in grave 2 is **Rose Zubrinich, 17 March 1860 – 24 September 1949** — the Rose Gormley he married at St Luke's in 1884, who **had no dates in this archive at all** and was born within a fortnight of her husband. In his own grave are **two of their children**, Susannah and Stanley, who died at eight years and at six months.

**Sixteen of the seventy-two are people on this site. Fifty-six are not** — and the plot numbers say who they were. *PRF, Lot 5, 10* holds Thomas Leo and a **Una Blanche** nobody here has heard of; *CR, Lot 44, 1* holds Arthur Leslie and a **Florence Johanna**; Broken Hill's *Catholic XC row 6 plot 33* holds Leonard James and an **Eveline Frances**. **A lot number is a household claim, and it is one a parish register cannot make.**

**Not one of the 72 is in Croatia.** Twenty-nine are at Port Pirie, thirteen at Enfield in Adelaide, six at **Timmins, Ontario** — which is where the 1928 Liverpool–Halifax arrival was going — four at Whyalla, two at Broken Hill, two in Pennsylvania, one in California.

And **Stanley J Zubrinich, a veteran, died 8 July 2001** at the South Australian Garden of Remembrance — very likely the Stanley Joseph who married in Queensland in 1947 and whom this archive could not place.

rows.src: Find a Grave — six dates checked against the tree
rows.what: Whether a cemetery index and a family tree disagree, and how
rows.got:
**Five of the six differences are not disagreements.** Find a Grave runs **one, two or ten days later** than the tree and **never earlier** — Susannah +1, Stanley +1, John William +2, Maurice Joseph +2, Arthur Leslie +10. That is the shape of a **burial**: a cemetery records the interment, a parish records the death, and the gap between them is the funeral. Read as conflicts they would have started five arguments; read as a pattern they are a lesson about what a cemetery index is.

**The sixth is real.** Leonard James died on **25 March** — both sources agree to the day — and the tree says **1985** where Broken Hill says **1983**. Same day, same month, two years apart, which is the shape of a typed digit. **This archive does not know which is right**, and says so. There is a photograph of the headstone on Find a Grave.

rows.src: Find a Grave — the Croatian cemeteries of this family
rows.what: Senj, Krivi Put, Karlobag, Otočac, Selce, Novi Vinodolski, Smokvica, Krmpote, Klenovica
rows.got:
**Every cemetery of this family that exists on Find a Grave is empty.**

*Gradsko groblje Senj – Sv. Vid* — **0 memorials**. *Krivi Put* — 0. *Groblje Karlobag* — 0. *Groblje Otočac* and *Otočac II* — 0 and 0. *Groblje Selce* — 0. *Groblje Novi Vinodolski* — 0. **Smokvica Krmpotska, Krmpote and Klenovica have no cemetery listed at all.**

Sixty-six Blažević memorials do exist in Croatia — almost all of them at **Mrkopalj** in Gorski Kotar and at Lovinac, which are other families.

The Senj entry is the sharp one: **this archive publishes a photograph of the Blažević plot in that cemetery**, with six names cut into it, and the world's largest index of gravestones has nothing there at all. What this archive holds is not a duplicate of a public record. It is the record.

rows.src: Arolsen Archives — the online collections themselves
rows.what: Codron of Rhodes, Defranceski, and the Senj deportations of 1943
rows.got:
**Tried and could not be reached from this machine.** `collections.arolsen-archives.org` refuses the connection here, in the browser and in a direct fetch alike, while `arolsen-archives.org` itself loads normally. That is this end, not theirs, and it is recorded rather than worked around.

**What is waiting there is worth saying out loud.** Hedviga's second husband, **Santou Isaac Codron, was born on Rhodes in 1913** — a Sephardic community of about 1,700 people that was deported to Auschwitz in **July 1944** and almost entirely destroyed. How he came to be alive to marry her in about 1973 is **the largest unanswered question in this archive**, and the Arolsen collections are the single most likely place to hold the answer. The three Arolsen cards this site already publishes reached it through a family tree, not through Arolsen.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj marriages 1888, all thirty-nine, end to end
rows.what: Juraj Blažević's marriage to Tereza Žubrinić, which the tree dates 1888
rows.got:
**The whole year is read and he is not in it.** 1888 runs from image 214 to image 221 and holds **39 marriages**, entry 1 on 12 January to entry 39 on 15 November. No Blažević married a Žubrinić at Senj that year. No Blažević married anyone.

That matters because **ahnentafel 4 has no birth date and no death date at all** — his wife has 1867–1931 and all four children have dates — and a marriage entry gives a groom's age, his father and his village in one line.

If they married in 1888 they married elsewhere, and the obvious elsewhere is the bride's parish: **Otočac, whose marriage register on film stops in 1872.** Krmpote has no marriage register filmed at all, Novi Vinodolski's stop in 1859, Ledenice's in 1882. **Three routes to this man's dates now end at the same wall.**

Three entries were worth carrying away regardless: *Vinko Antić × Julka Vukelić* on 21 June — two of this archive's surnames marrying each other at Senj — *Martin Kozina × Anjelika Boras* in January, and *Josip Draženović × Marija Jovanović of Otočac* in September.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj baptisms, image 55 (the lead attached to ahnentafel 4)
rows.what: «Potentially him? 1861?» — a citation sitting unopened in Juraj Blažević's own record
rows.got:
**Opened, read at full resolution, and it is a different family.**

Page 50 of the Senj baptismal register, entry 55: **Georgius**, born **22 April 1861**, baptised 28 April, *legitimus* — father **Antonius Blažević, *mercator***, mother **Anna nata Trbuhović**.

Ahnentafel 4's father is **Toma Blažević, a *nadničar***, a day labourer of Smokvica Krmpotska, who in 1861 was twenty-three. The name and the year fit; the father does not, and **the father decides**.

The citation had been carried in the tree since 2014 with a question mark on it. Answering a question mark is worth as much as finding something, and this one is now answered.

rows.src: FamilySearch — the record index, for everything it holds on ahnentafel 4
rows.what: Every indexed Croatian church record naming Juraj Blažević with Tereza Žubrinić
rows.got:
**Three records, and this archive had already read all three** — Ljubomir's marriage of 1920, Anka's of 1919, and Marijan's baptism at Krmpote in 1895. He is a name in the parents' column of each and none gives his age.

**One small new thing:** at Marijan's baptism the priest wrote him **Ivko** — a fourth form of the name, beside Juraj, Jurko and Georgius.

The negative is the useful part: **the Senj marriage film is not indexed for 1888**, so finding anything in it means reading it, which is what was then done.

rows.src: Matricula Online
rows.what: Every parish of this family, and Rhodes, against the whole portal
rows.got:
**Matricula holds no Croatian registers at all.** Its fonds are Germany (9,123), Austria (2,857), Slovenia (723), Switzerland (292), Luxembourg (277), Italy (106), Poland, Serbia, Bosnia — and **there is no Croatia entry**. The Italian holdings are Reggio Calabria and Bolzano-Brixen; nothing Istrian, nothing on the Kvarner.

Searched by place all the same, because a fonds list is a claim and a search is a test: **Senj, Otočac, Karlobag, Krmpote, Novi Vinodolski, Crikvenica, Rijeka, Fiume, Gospić — nothing.** *Selce* and *Brinje* return hits that are Slovenian villages of the same name, and *Kroatien* matches a parish in Regensburg. **Rhodes returns nothing**, which closes it for Hedviga's second husband too.

The method was checked against a control — *Wien* returns a hundred parishes — so this is the portal's coverage and not a broken query. **Matricula can be struck off the list for this family**, and that is worth writing down once so nobody spends an evening on it again.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj marriages, 1859–1920
rows.what: Every Papić and Blažević marriage the film holds, read page by page
rows.got:
**Eleven marriages, and every other bride on each page.** Pages 303, 307, 315, 322, 324, 326, 333, 348, 350, 355, 359 and — at full resolution on 13 September — 192, 294 and 366.

The pages carry more than the family. **The tobacco factory shows up as a decade-long trend**: three of five brides in 1909 give *tvorničarka* as their occupation, seven of eight by 1919. That is not a household fact; it is an industrial one, and it is only visible because the whole page was read rather than the one entry.

The film was also **verified end to end** — image 196 is page 192 (1885), image 371 is page 366 (1920).

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj marriages, 1734–1858
rows.what: Juraj Papa × Matija Filipić, and every marriage above them
rows.got:
**The older Senj marriage book has never been opened.** It is the volume that would carry ahnentafel 12's own marriage — Juraj “Papa” Antić of Selce to Matija Filipić — and with it the join between the Selce house and the Senj one.

It is held, it is filmed, and nothing but sitting hours stands between this archive and it.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj deaths, 1859–1907
rows.what: Two entries, and what the pages around them say about how people died
rows.got:
**Toma Blažević, tuberculosis, aged 69 (p.162, 1903)** and **Stanko Papić, scarlatina at twenty months (p.225, 1907)** — the second in an outbreak that killed four children in eight days.

Two pages of one register. **Everything else in the Senj death books is unread**, and the archive's own name-reuse table leans on that silence without saying so.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj deaths, 1915 · Senj baptisms, Jan–Feb 1895
rows.what: Zvonimir Vukelić's death; the two sisters recorded eighteen days apart
rows.got:
**Not in this collection, and the catalogue said otherwise.** Senj deaths on film stop at **1907**; Senj births stop at **1894**. Both sisters fall one year outside, and the death that widowed Milka at twenty-eight falls eight years outside.

Four published research plans depended on these two books. They were written against a catalogue label, and checking the film killed all four in an afternoon. That is the most useful negative this archive has recorded.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Senj baptisms, 1734–1894
rows.what: Milka Papić's baptism, 1886
rows.got:
**Her own baptism at str. 122** — and a registrar's margin added in **1971** citing her death entry at page 280, line 37. A parish clerk closed the loop eighty-five years later and left the reference behind for us.

**Her eight siblings' baptisms are attached in the tree as images and none has been read.**

rows.src: FamilySearch — Krmpote-Vodice (sv. Jakov) births, the film behind the label
rows.what: Whether the film really holds 1815–1896, as the waypoint claims
rows.got:
**The label is wrong by sixty-four years.** Image 10 is page 2 and reads *Godine 1879*; image 188 is page 177 and reads *Godine 1896*. **The film is 1879–1896.**

This is the parish that should hold every Blažević above Toma, and Jurko Blažević — born about the 1860s — is outside it. Two published plans died here as well. The lesson has been written into the harvest map: *the label on a waypoint is a claim about the parish, not about the film.*

rows.src: FamilySearch — Krmpote (sv. Jakov) baptisms, 1888 and 1895
rows.what: The Blažević children of Smokvica krmpotska 114
rows.got:
**Two children born at the same house number seven years apart**, HDA 111 p.104 and HDA 176 p.168 — and **two different men called Ivo Blažević** standing godfather, one the son of Mate and one the son of Toma.

That is what made the archive stop calling Smokvica 114 a household. **It is a zadruga** — an extended family under one roof and one number — and the correction runs through every page that counted people by house.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Krivi Put baptisms, 1859
rows.what: Antonija Perpić, Krivi Put N° 136
rows.got:
Her household is entered ***Confiniarii*** — **a Military Frontier family**, which is a legal status and not a description. Seven Perpić children sit on the one page.

Only the page her entry falls on has been opened.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Otočac baptisms, 1834 and 1845
rows.what: The Žubrinić household at Šumećica 24
rows.got:
**Nicolaus, 1834, at Šumećica 24, *Confiniarius*** — and a **Josephus in 1845 whose mother is née Marković where the 1834 mother is née Orešković.** Five Frontier offices came out of the godparent columns of two pages.

The two mothers are the whole of question 4d: **one Michaël Žubrinić with two wives, or two men of the same name.** The books that would settle it — Otočac marriages before 1834, and deaths 1834–45 — are unopened.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Otočac, Stanje duša (status animarum) 1710–1846
rows.what: The Žubrinić households of Šumećica 2 and 24, listed by house rather than by event
rows.got:
**The right instrument, and still unread.** A household census lists *Pagus, Domus, Nomina Familiæ* and birth dates together — it is the one document that would show a Žubrinić household whole instead of one baptism at a time, and it reaches back **a hundred and twenty-four years before the baptismal register begins.**

The film target is confirmed. The reading has been split into a session of its own because it is a week of work, not an afternoon.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Otočac marriages, 1859–1872
rows.what: Whether the 1859 marriage on the film is ahnentafel 10's
rows.got:
Images 129–147 verified against their printed pages — pag. 10 is 1862, pag. 18 is 1865. **One entry read out in full and deliberately not claimed.** On 14 September the identification was revised *down*: the 1859 marriage is now **less** likely to be his, and the note says so rather than quietly dropping it.

The register has no column this archive wanted: **it does not give the fathers' villages.**

rows.src: FamilySearch — Karlobag baptisms, 1754–1838
rows.what: Every Karlobag ancestor on the direct line
rows.got:
**Seven pages, and the best-read parish in the archive.** A *Dominus* honorific, a Giustiniani godfather, a Pro-Colonel, a Captain, a Baron von Holstein — and one volume kept in **Croatian rather than Latin**.

Two sittings in September closed two more: **ahnentafel 27's baptism of 1810**, confirming the tree to the day, and **ahnentafel 13's of 18 September 1838**, which gave the archive its first people who worked at sea — her father a *cammeralis nauclerus*, a chamber shipmaster, and her grandfather a *mercator*.

Both readings nearly went wrong. The 1810 month read as *7ma* — September — at page scale and is a **ditto mark** at 3.4×; it would have been published as a five-month correction to a tree that was right.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Selce baptisms, 1806 (the page long labelled Vrbnik)
rows.what: Which parish ahnentafel 24's baptism actually belongs to
rows.got:
**The parish is Selce, not Vrbnik — and this archive carried the wrong label for weeks** on the strength of a modern pencil annotation.

What settled it was not the page but the priest. The baptism is signed *“Mich: Rombol Capell: Loci”*; the **Selce deaths of 1806**, on a different film, are kept by the same man under the same title. Same hand, same office, same year.

The page also answered question 5: three underlined by-names in one entry — ***Antich Papa*, *Loncsarich Franich*, *Antich Dudin***.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Selce baptisms, 1809 and 1838
rows.what: Ahnentafel 25's baptism, and ahnentafel 12's
rows.got:
**1809, entry 70, house 110** — the tree's 22 March confirmed, ahnentafel 50 and 51 named, and a ninth by-name pair, *“Jellichich dictis Jurešina”*, underlined by the priest exactly as his successor underlined *“Antich Papa”* a generation later.

**1838, image 186, domus 51** — ahnentafel 12's own baptism on 11 March, the tree's exact date, in the same house as his parents' marriage three years before and by the same priest. His father is entered *“Josephi Antich Papa”*, which carries the by-name to the font.

One thing got worse: **the child's name is written *Gregorium*, not *Georgium*.** The identification is beyond doubt; the given name now is not.

Both volumes were **on disk the whole time**, attached in the tree and counted merely as *scanned*.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Selce marriages, 1835
rows.what: Ahnentafel 24's marriage to ahnentafel 25
rows.got:
**Four direct ancestors named in one entry** — 48, 49, 50 and 51, all four already dead — at houses 51 and 80, pages 21–22.

The groom is entered *“Josephum Antich Papa”*; his sister, marrying the bride's brother **the same day**, is *“Euphemia Antich aliter Papa”*. **Five more *aliter* pairs sit on the same opening.** This is the page that turned a curiosity into a system.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Selce deaths, 1832 and 1842
rows.what: The nine direct ancestors this book should hold
rows.got:
**Two found, both confirming the tree to the day and both adding a house number it did not have.** Ahnentafel 50: *“Die 1ª Aprilis 1832”*, house 39, *“Georgius Jellicich, Antonii”* — a patronymic that names his father. Ahnentafel 51: *“Die 8ª Maji 1842”*, entry 147, house 204.

**The archive had published a question claiming the register contradicted the tree here. It did not.** The question was withdrawn and the reason stated: the tree was reached for as the likely culprit because it usually is — which is a bias, not an argument.

**Seven more direct ancestors are in this book and its companion**, and the two houses — 39 and 204 — still do not match.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Novi Vinodolski, the 1650 register
rows.what: Whether the oldest register in reach is readable at all
rows.got:
**The label holds and the hand is the surprise.** The film target says 1650–1786 and the earliest leaves are **in Croatian, not Latin** — the glagolitic littoral's own practice, a century before the Latin registers this archive is used to.

**One hundred and twenty events** from this family are reachable in the Novi Vinodolski books. Nobody has read a line of them.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Grižane, Stanje duša 1738
rows.what: A second household census, older than Otočac's and in another parish
rows.got:
**Household lists in Croatian, at images ~100–140 of a 579-image film** — and **the by-names again, in 1738, in a parish a day's walk from the others.** The practice this archive documented across ten surnames between 1806 and 1885 is visibly older and wider than its evidence.

**The Blaževići on this page are not claimed.** They are Blaževići at Grižane in 1738 and nothing yet joins them to this family.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Brinje births, marriages and deaths 1888–1900
rows.what: Kalanj, Perković and Borić, three surnames that meet inland over the Kapela
rows.got: **Not one page of the Brinje register has ever been opened, and Brinje is not in this archive's gazetteer.** It got onto the list because a 1910 American manifest gave a Kalanj's residence as Brinje, which sent someone back to re-read a Latin baptism of 1864: *“Brinjensis parochiae ruricolae”* — country people of the parish of Brinje, forty kilometres inland from the coast where this archive had always put them.

rows.src: FamilySearch — Rijeka registers
rows.what: Ljubomir Blažević's baptism, 1891–92
rows.got: **Never checked — not even the holdings.** Question 13 rests on it, and the parish has sat in the harvest map marked *NOT CHECKED* since the map was written.

rows.src: FamilySearch — the image viewer at full resolution
rows.what: Whether a 5,768-pixel register scan can be read without a person at the keyboard
rows.got:
**This archive twice published that it could not be done, and was twice wrong.** The Deep Zoom tiles do 401 and taint the canvas — **from `sg30p0.familysearch.org`.** The same tiles are served from **`www.familysearch.org`**, which is same-origin with the viewer: no preflight, no tainted canvas, cookies sent.

So the register can be read at **six times** the resolution of the 960-pixel copies this archive had been squinting at, and the method is committed as a tool rather than retold each time.

It matters more than it sounds. At page scale a **19 reads as 1**, a flat-topped **2 reads as 7**, and *Prpić* reads as *Papić*. Two of those nearly reached this site as corrections to a tree that was right.

rows.src: FamilySearch — access denied, Error 15
rows.what: Two sessions of tile fetching, and what happened next
rows.got:
**The site stopped answering.** After two long sessions and heavy tile traffic the viewer returned *Access Denied, Error 15*.

Work stopped rather than retried from another angle. The symptoms and the avoidance are written down in `tools/familysearch.md` so the next session paces itself. Access returned the following day.

rows.src: MyHeritage — the family tree export
rows.what: The 15,643-person tree that every page here is built from
rows.got:
**The spine of the archive, and the thing it is most careful about.** One GEDCOM feeds seven sibling archives. It is not evidence — it is somebody's assembled belief, and this site's whole method is to say which parts of it a document actually holds up.

Where it has been checked against a register it has been **right far more often than wrong**, including on dates this archive briefly tried to correct.

rows.src: MyHeritage — every image attached to every person
rows.what: What is already on disk and has never been read out
rows.got:
**Repeatedly the best source in the building.** The 1835 Selce marriage, the 1809 baptism and the 1838 baptism were each “awaiting a trip to Croatia” and each was already attached to the tree at 2,987 pixels.

The same sweep turned up **three Arolsen Archives cards** filed under Hedviga's husband that nobody had opened, and they place him in a Württemberg factory at sixteen.

The coverage tool now separates *scanned* from *read*, because the difference was hiding a dozen documents in plain sight.

rows.src: FindMyPast — ZUBRINICH, the first spelling
rows.what: Every record under the anglicised spelling — manifests, marriages, rolls
rows.got:
**Ivan Žubrinić's 1884 marriage at St Luke, Port Pirie names his father** — civil confirmation of a link this archive held only from the tree — and gives his wife **Rose Garmly** a father, **Thomas Garmly**, where she previously had no parents at all.

**Mate Žubrinić of Prozor 50**, whose record here stopped at his birth in 1867, **sailed to New York in 1911** leaving a wife, Roza.

And the method finding that shaped everything after: **post-1906 American manifests carry a last residence and the relative left behind.** That is a Croatian village, named by the emigrant, in an English-language index.

rows.src: FindMyPast — ZUBRINIC, the second spelling
rows.what: 106 of 119 records read as transcripts rather than index rows
rows.got:
**Šumećica is an emigration village and this archive did not know it.** *Franjo Zubrinic, b. 1883, Noordam, 1910, residence “Sumenica”, wife left behind, brother already in New York.* Šumećica is ahnentafel 10's own hamlet, and the archive's emigration page had **Prozor and nothing else**.

Three Otočac men, one naming his **father Marko**; a Prozor man naming his **father Sandro**; and the **Kostelac** link — a nephew and an uncle of that name meeting two different Žubrinići off two different ships.

Also a warning worth as much as the finds: **only the `ELLIS2` dataset carries residence and relations.** Records whose id begins `R_` or `US/PASSENGERLISTS` will not tell you where in Croatia anyone came from, and the `…/2` and `…/3` suffixes are **relations named on a record, not passengers** — they surface in the index as though they had travelled.

rows.src: FindMyPast — the Kalanj emigration
rows.what: Where the Klenovica Kalanji went, and where they came from
rows.got:
**The one finding that changed the Croatian research.** A 1910 manifest gave a Kalanj's residence as **Brinje**; the re-read of their own 1864 baptism then said the same thing in Latin. **They are not a Klenovica family.**

Three of this archive's surnames meet at Brinje — **Kalanj, Perković and Borić** — and a Borić of Brinje married a Papić of Senj.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Canadian arrivals and the St Albans border crossings
rows.what: Three Žubrinić women into Saint John and Halifax, 1926–1930
rows.got:
**Found, and thin on purpose.** Mauda (*Montrose*, Saint John NB, 11 Feb 1926), Nikdla (*Regina*, Halifax, 28 Mar 1928) and Vinka (*Minnedosa*, Saint John NB, 19 Feb 1930) all sailed from Liverpool — and these are **UK outbound lists, which do not name a Croatian village.**

The **St Albans, Vermont** border crossings are thinner still: country of birth and nothing else. Recording that is the point — it stops the next person spending a subscription day on a seam that cannot carry what they need.

rows.src: FindMyPast — Port Pirie electoral rolls
rows.what: Nineteen roll entries for the Žubrinići of South Australia
rows.got: **Eleven of nineteen read; the trial expires before the rest.** Rolls give an address and an occupation year by year, which is how a household is watched moving rather than merely found.

rows.src: Ancestry
rows.what: Nothing. This archive has never run a search there
rows.got: **Zero searches, and it is the obvious hole beside FindMyPast.** Its Australian, South African and American sets overlap only partly with what has been read, and the people this archive most needs to follow — the ones who left — are exactly the ones it indexes.

rows.src: Arolsen Archives — the three cards already on disk
rows.what: Three ITS index cards attached to Hedviga's husband and never opened
rows.got:
**A sixteen-year-old in a Württemberg factory.** *Iwan/Jvan Defranceski*, born **25 June 1925 at Crikvenica** — the same day and place as the 1951 Yugoslav birth extract — lodging at **Pfullingen, Brunnenstraße 7**, working as a *Hilfsarbeiter* for **Licht u. Kraft, Reutlingen** from **21 October 1941**, and stamped *DOCUMENT EXPLOITÉ* by the French occupation authority.

The cards came through the family tree, not through Arolsen. **Nobody had ever searched the Arolsen collections themselves.**

rows.src: Državni arhiv u Gospiću — asked, acknowledged, queued
rows.what: Three asks: the Kalanj × Perković marriage at Brinje; Otočac baptisms for Prozor 1875–1895; the one-man-or-two question
rows.got:
**Sent 13 September 2026 to zahtjevi@arhiv-gospic.hr, and acknowledged the next day** by **Marija Fajdić, viši arhivist, Voditelj Odjela**: *«potvrđujemo primitak vašeg zahtjeva. O njegovu rješavanju bit ćete pravodobno obaviješteni kada vaš zahtjev dođe na red za obradu.»*

A queue acknowledgement with a named archivist. **Still open.** The three asks are unchanged — the **Kalanj × Perković marriage at Brinje**, **Otočac baptisms for Prozor 1875–1895**, and the **one-man-or-two question** — and each was written with names, years and house numbers rather than as a general enquiry, because that is the kind an archivist can answer in an afternoon.

rows.src: Državni arhiv u Rijeci, Ispostava u Senju — asked, and answered
rows.what: Jurko Blažević at Sv. Jakov Krmpote; Zvonimir Vukelić's death of 1915; the Butorac household
rows.got:
**A nil return with a map, answered in a day.** Denis Rukavina, 14 September 2026: *«**Sabirni centar u Senju nema u svom posjedu arhivsku građu kojom bi se moglo udovoljiti Vašem zahtjevu.** S istim zahtjevom obratite se **Državnom arhivu u Rijeci**, **Državnom arhivu u Gospiću** i **nadležnim Župnim uredima**.»*

The Senj outpost **does not hold this material** — and that is now known rather than assumed. **Three doors are named in its place**, and one of them, **the parish offices**, is a route this archive has never tried at all. The Krmpote registers after 1896 and the Senj ones after 1907 are in **parish custody or at Rijeka**.

It does not touch the four plans the film ranges killed. Those books exist; this only changes which address holds them. **A third letter — to Rijeka, and to the Župni ured of Sv. Jakov Krmpote and of Senj — is the obvious next move and is not yet written.**

rows.src: Southern Rhodesian immigration, 1953–65
rows.what: Twenty-two years of Hedviga's life
rows.got: **An entire country known from two words on a later record.** No route into it has been identified yet, which is a different thing from having searched and found nothing — and this row exists so the difference stays visible.

rows.src: The archive's own attached media — read against the coverage grade
rows.what: Whether “scanned” and “read” were being counted as the same thing
rows.got:
**They were, and it flattered the archive.** A person could be graded *scanned* — an image attached, nothing read out — while the document had in fact been read weeks earlier, because a reading lives in prose and not in data.

A file of readings now carries the citation for every document actually read out. **Read went from 19 to 31 and scanned from 12 to zero**, which is not progress: it is the same evidence, counted honestly.

rows.src: The archive's own claim that 63 scans were unreferenced
rows.what: A number this archive published about itself
rows.got: **The true figure is zero.** The 63 was an artefact of searching by filename. It was caught before it deployed, and it is recorded here because an archive that logs only its external searches will keep believing its own arithmetic.

rows.src: Every published person matched to the register that would hold their events
rows.what: How much of this family is reachable in filmed parish books, and where
rows.got:
**519 events are reachable** — births, marriages and deaths whose parish is known and whose book is filmed and in range.

**One hundred and thirty-nine of them appeared only after the village parser was fixed.** House numbers were sitting inside the village field — *“Klenovica 22”*, *“#6 Mrzli Dol”* — and every person so recorded was invisible to the match. A parsing bug had been hiding a fifth of the harvest.

rows.src: The by-name phrases, gathered across ten surnames
rows.what: Every *aliter*, *dictus* and *dicti* the read pages carry
rows.got:
**Sixteen phrases, thirteen pairs, ten surnames, 1806–1885 — and eight of them underlined by the scribe.** The underline is the tell: the priest is marking the household name, not decorating.

It makes *Antić* and *Papić* one family rather than two, and it is the reason this archive can read a Senj marriage of 1885 and a Selce baptism of 1806 as the same line.
